Based on Erwin F. Lange, 'Alchemy and the Sixteenth Century Metallurgists,' Ambix 13:2 (1966) pp.92-95; and Anneliese G. persons.name: Vannoccio Biringuccio
persons.bio_html:
Vannoccio Biringuccio (1480–1539) was a Sienese metallurgist, mining engineer, and technical writer whose De la Pirotechnia (Venice, 1540) was the first comprehensive printed treatise on metallurgy and practical chemistry in European history. Born in Siena and closely associated with the Petrucci family that dominated that city's politics, Biringuccio traveled widely in Italy and Germany during his career, visiting mining operations, foundries, and metallurgical installations across Central Europe. He spent his final years in Rome as head of the Papal foundry and munitions works — an appointment that reflected both the practical importance of his knowledge and the growing role of technical expertise in early modern statecraft and warfare.

De la Pirotechnia, published posthumously by Curtio Navo in Venice in 1540 under the auspices of the Pope, the Holy Roman Emperor, and the Venetian Senate, described in unprecedented detail the assaying, reducing, and alloying of metals including gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, iron, mercury, and antimony; the preparation of mineral acids, saltpetre, and gunpowder; and a wide range of metallurgical processes from distillation to bell-casting, wire-drawing, and coin-minting. Erwin F. Lange, in Ambix (1966), identifies Biringuccio as one of the earliest scientific writers to systematically critique the transmutational claims of alchemy on empirical grounds: he devoted twelve pages of the Pirotechnia to the subject, arguing from observation and experiment that he had been 'unable to observe any cases where alchemists became rich because of the practice,' and noting that while alchemy's methods were futile for producing gold, they had yielded valuable results in medicinals, dyestuffs, and other useful substances. This balanced critique — rejecting gold-making while crediting ancillary chemical achievements — anticipates the attitude toward alchemy taken by later chemists including Robert Boyle. The Pirotechnia appeared in Italian, French, and English, with the first reliable English translation by Cyril Stanley Smith and Martha Teach Gnudi published in 1942 and reprinted by Basic Books in 1959.

persons.name: Lazarus Ercker
persons.bio_html:
Lazarus Ercker (d. 1593) was a German metallurgist and mining administrator in the service of Rudolf II, Holy Roman Emperor, who served as chief superintendent of the mines in the kingdom of Bohemia and authored the most important sixteenth-century treatise on assaying and ore-testing. Ercker worked alongside Rudolf II's other court scholars and specialists, including the astronomers Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler, in the environment of Prague's intellectually cosmopolitan court. Erwin F. Lange, in Ambix (1966), identifies Ercker as the third of the major sixteenth-century metallurgists after Biringuccio and Agricola, and notes that his work 'might well be considered an important forerunner of books dealing with chemical quantitative analysis.' His approach was strictly empirical: Ercker declined to discuss alchemical transmutation beyond dismissing 'the cements used by the philosophers and alchemists to change copper to silver and silver to gold' with the terse observation that he would 'leave them for what they were worth' and deal only with 'processes and procedures which had been thoroughly tested and could be relied upon.'

His principal work, Beschreibung Allerfürnemsten Mineralischen Erzt-und Bergwerkarten (Description of the Foremost Mineral Ores and Mining Operations), first published in Prague in the German language, went through multiple editions and translations, with an early English translation by Sir John Pettus in 1683 considered unreliable. The modern scholarly translation by Anneliese G. Sisco and Cyril Stanley Smith, published by the University of Chicago Press in 1951 as Lazarus Ercker's Treatise on Ores and Assaying, made Ercker's work accessible to modern scholars. The work is notable for its practical instructions not only in the assaying of gold, silver, copper, and other metals, but also in the construction of precision instruments including the analytical balance — which Ercker described fashioning from a sword blade — and standardized sets of weights, reflecting the early modern concern with quantitative measurement in metallurgical and chemical practice.

events.title: Lazarus Ercker Publishes Treatise on Ores and Assaying in Prague Under Rudolf II
events.description: Around 1574, Lazarus Ercker (d. 1593), chief superintendent of the mines in the kingdom of Bohemia under Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II, published his Beschreibung Allerfürnemsten Mineralischen Erzt-und Bergwerkarten (Description of the Foremost Mineral Ores and Mining Operations) in Prague. Erwin F. Lange, in Ambix (1966), identifies Ercker's treatise as the third of the major sixteenth-century metallurgical works, alongside Biringuccio's Pirotechnia (1540) and Agricola's De re Metallica (1556), that together established an empirical tradition of mining and metallurgical knowledge distinct from the transmutational claims of alchemy. Like Biringuccio and Agricola, Ercker dismissed alchemical gold-making with terse practicality, confining himself to 'processes and procedures which had been thoroughly tested and could be relied upon.' The work's particular contribution was in quantitative assaying and analytical procedure: it provided detailed instructions for the assaying of gold, silver, and copper; for making precision instruments including the analytical balance (which Ercker described fashioning from a sword blade); and for constructing and calibrating standardized sets of weights. Sisco and Smith, in their English translation (University of Chicago Press, 1951), identify the work as a forerunner of modern quantitative chemical analysis. Ercker worked at the court of Rudolf II alongside Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler, in a milieu that combined empirical metallurgical expertise with the astrology, Paracelsian medicine, and alchemical speculation that Rudolf famously patronized. The Beschreibung went through multiple editions and translations, including an early English version by Sir John Pettus in 1683.
events.scholarly_grounding: Erwin F. Lange identifies Lazarus Ercker and his Beschreibung Allerfürnemsten Mineralischen Erzt-und Bergwerkarten (Prague, ca. 1574) as the third of the major sixteenth-century metallurgists and their work as representative of an empirical tradition opposed to alchemical transmutation, in 'Alchemy and the Sixteenth Century Metallurgists,' Ambix 13:2 (1966) pp.92-95. See also Anneliese G. Sisco and Cyril Stanley Smith, Lazarus Ercker's Treatise on Ores and Assaying (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1951).
